title: Looking back: the long hymns
hookLine: Sukhmani, Asa di Var, Barah Maha and the ninth Guru's saloks

lines: SOME PRAYERS FIT IN A BREATH.
cards: Some prayers fit in a breath. Others take an hour and more, and people make room for them anyway.
In some Sikh families, when someone is ill or a home is starting something new, relatives gather on the floor to read Sukhmani Sahib together, start to finish, passing it along.
In gurdwaras before sunrise, ragis are already singing a ballad that runs until the sky goes pale. Long hymns ask for time, and often company. This year gave you four.

teach.b: First, Sukhmani Sahib, Guru Arjan's psalm of peace, in Raga Gauri: twenty-four ashtpadis, each opening with a salok and then eight stanzas. Some read it whole; some read a part each day.
Its refrain names the whole hymn: sukhmani sukh amrit prabh naam, the jewel of peace is God's ambrosial Name, the resting place of the devotees' minds.
This path spent a hundred days on it, longer than on anything else this year.

teach.h: ASA DI VAR: A BALLAD AT DAWN.
teach.b: Second, Asa di Var, Guru Nanak's ballad for dawn. A var was a hero's ballad, sung about kings and battles.
Guru Nanak took the form and turned it inward: twenty-four pauris, with saloks of Guru Nanak and Guru Angad, and in the gurdwara Guru Ram Das's chhants sung between them.
Its first salok is gratitude: balihaaree gur aapne, a sacrifice to my Guru, a hundred times a day.

teach.h: BARAH MAHA: TWELVE MONTHS OF LONGING.
teach.b: Third, the Barah Maha, Guru Arjan's twelve months in Raga Majh. In the old Punjabi form, a woman longs for her absent beloved as the seasons turn; here the longing is the soul's, for God.
It opens with people separated by their own deeds, asking in mercy to be united, and Sikhs read it in gurdwaras on Sangrand.

Fourth, the saloks of Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, near the very end of the Granth: short, calm couplets about a world that passes and a Name that stays. One says the wise person frightens no one and fears no one.

Four long hymns, four moods: peace, gratitude, longing, steadiness. And this week has been a look back of its own: the Gurus' gurpurabs, the first installation, the Granth made Guru, and the daily banis.

how: Many Sikhs read Sukhmani Sahib daily or in family gatherings, gurdwaras sing Asa di Var before sunrise, the Barah Maha is read on Sangrand, and Guru Tegh Bahadur's saloks are read near the close of a full reading of the Granth.

games.q: the long hymns — tap the pairs.
p: Guru Nanak's ballad, sung at dawn
calm couplets near the Granth's end

s: Asa di Var is sung late at night in gurdwaras
it's sung at dawn, before sunrise, with Guru Ram Das's chhants between the pauris.
each of Sukhmani's twenty-four ashtpadis opens with a salok
a salok, then eight stanzas: that's the pattern all the way through.
the Barah Maha is read in gurdwaras on Sangrand
the first day of each month, its month's stanza is read.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. a var is a ballad sung about kings and battles. what do you do with the form?
o: use it for the inner life and praise of God.
write a ballad about a well-known battle.
games.why: Asa di Var keeps the ballad's shape, twenty-four pauris, but its battles are inward, and it opens in gratitude to the Guru.

practice: Peace, gratitude, longing or steadiness: pick the one you need today, and find a few lines of it in a gutka, a gurbani app, or simply in memory.
Read them slowly, twice, and let one phrase come back now and then, like a tune you can't shake. If you pray, you can let those lines carry your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Looking back. Four long hymns side by side: Sukhmani's peace, Asa di Var's gratitude, the Barah Maha's longing, and the ninth Guru's steady saloks.

orig.note: Punjabi: the jewel of peace, the name of Guru Arjan's long hymn in Raga Gauri.

carryVoice: Your line: the long hymns. Some things are worth the whole hour. Another week, done.
